primal, your brain's need to feel safe. If you've got a desk where you can't focus, a bed where you toss and turn, or a beautiful sofa you never actually want to sit on, the reason might not be your taste. It might be your layout. [music] And the idea here comes from what's

known as prospect-refuge theory, which says that we're wired to feel best in spots where we can see what's coming while our back is protected. And it's not hard to understand why. Just think about early humans. The safest place for them wasn't in the middle of an open field. It was the edge of a forest or a shallow cave, places where you can see the open landscape in front of you, which is your prospect, while having a solid surface behind you, which is your refuge. And even though we live in modern homes with locks and lights, your nervous system still responds the same way. We relax when our view is open and our back feels protected. And you can

see this most clearly in children. They're not scared of their bedroom, they're scared of the blind spots, the closet, the hallway, and under the bed. So, kids call it monsters, but adults call it, "I just can't relax in this room." But it's the same feeling, which brings me to one of the most common layout mistakes I see in homes. We put ourselves in positions where we can't see what's behind us. For example, a lot of people set up a home office desk facing a wall, which means that they've got their back to the doorway for 8 hours a day. Or they drop a sofa in the middle of the room, so the main walkway is directly behind them. And no, you're not literally thinking that a predator

is going to come and eat you, but your brain still treats that blind spot as a problem. And your amygdala, which is the part of your brain that detects threats, it stays switched on, spending energy monitoring what you can't see behind you. And so you don't necessarily feel fear, but what you do feel is restlessness, trouble focusing, tension in your body, and the urge to get up and leave the room for no reason. So, if a room looks good but never feels good, this is usually why. So, here's how to fix it. >> [music] >> You want to set up a few key spots in a command position. So first, walk through your home and identify the main locations where you spend the most time.

So, for most of us that's going to be your desk chair, your sofa, and the head of your bed. And then for each one, aim for two things. Number one, a solid backing, so a wall or something else substantial and solid directly behind you. And then number two, a clear view where you can see the room's primary entry point from where you sit or lie down. But what do you do if that doesn't make sense for your space? Like, what if you're floating a sofa in an open concept living room and you don't want to jam it up against the wall? No problem. In that situation, you want to create some artificial refuge to calm your brain. So, put a solid console behind the sofa, and then give it some

visual weight in the form of tall lamps, stacked books, and a large plant. And pro tip, dense foliage works especially well here. Because all that creates a psychological barrier that tells your nervous system, "My back is protected, so I can relax." But I want you to notice, this isn't a renovation. Just by shifting your furniture into a real command position, you reduce that low-level threat response, so the room feels more relaxing, your focus gets stronger, and your body loses the tension because you finally gave your brain the feeling of safety it's been craving. But once your room feels safe, there's a

second problem that inevitably comes up, and it's the reason one nice upgrade can turn into a full-blown spending spiral. Because have you ever finally saved up for one beautiful, expensive piece, but then the second you bring it home, it

feels like it made your whole room look worse? Like you splurge on a sleek, modern velvet sofa, and as soon as you set it down, suddenly your vintage coffee table looks cheap, the rug you used to love now looks tattered, [music] and even the curtains feel outdated. And you get this almost magnetic urge to replace everything else just to match the sofa. And you're not being dramatic, you're just experiencing something psychologists call the Diderot effect. And there's a little bit of history behind this one. Back in the 1700s, the French philosopher Denis Diderot was gifted a luxurious scarlet robe, and he loved that robe until he wore it in his study. Because once that robe was in the room, everything else looked shabby by comparison. The desk, the chairs, and

all his decor. And the mismatch bothered him so much that he slowly replaced item after item and ended up under a mountain of debt. And that's why we call it the Diderot effect. When one new, higher-status item changes your baseline, and now everything around it feels like it has to level up. So, fast forward to now, and this is how the furniture industry makes a lot of its money because we crave a sense of cohesion in our environment. So when you introduce a piece that speaks a totally different style language, whether it's new versus old, formal versus casual, or sleek versus rustic, your brain recognizes that as friction, and it tries to fix that friction the fastest way it knows how, by buying more stuff.

But the goal isn't to stop buying nice things. The goal is to stop one nice thing from forcing everything else to audition for its job. And the way out of this is to design with bridge pieces, materials and objects that make different styles look like they belong together. Because if your room is perfectly matched with everything in the same wood tone or looking like it came from the same store, then any new piece sticks out immediately. There's no flexibility. Instead, you want to build a baseline that can absorb changes by mixing textures and finishes on purpose. And so some examples of bridge materials that work almost every time are raw or weathered wood, aged brass, distressed leather, heavily textured linen, and stone or ceramics with some visible

variation. These materials act like visual buffers, and they tell your brain, "This room has layers, not a single catalog identity." So for example, a polished modern chrome lamp looks weird on a cheap laminate table, but put that same lamp on a scarred antique wood table, suddenly it looks well curated. So learn to leverage bridge pieces so you can add that one beautiful upgrade without triggering the feeling of needing to replace everything. But even if you beat the Diderot effect and arrange your furniture into a solid command position, your room can still make you feel on edge. And this is something a lot of people miss because so many people think about interior design as something purely visual. But your home isn't just something you look

at. It's also something you hear and feel. And you already know this feeling. You walk into a room that looks beautiful, but it feels oddly tense. Like every footstep is loud, every chair scrape hits your nerves, and even the clink of a glass feels sharp. Because a room can be gorgeous and perfectly balanced on paper and still spike your stress if it sounds wrong. And the reason comes down to how your brain filters noise through a process called sensory gating. Sensory gating is your brain's noise filter. It blocks out safe, repetitive background sounds so you can focus and relax. It's why you stop noticing the refrigerator hum after a few minutes. And in a quiet, acoustically soft room, your brain can block out the small stuff really easily,

and your nervous system actually settles. The problem is that modern design has been trending toward flat, reflective surfaces. >> [music] >> So people rip out carpet for hardwood or vinyl plank, and they choose smooth drywall, bare windows, glass, metal, and minimal decor. And so it all looks clean

and nice in photos, but acoustically, it can turn your home into an echo chamber. Because in rooms full of hard surfaces, sound doesn't get absorbed. It bounces. [music] And that creates sharp, high-frequency reverberations that are completely unpredictable, and your brain has a much harder time filtering that out. So every footstep, every chair scrape, and every clink on a stone countertop lands like a little jolt, and your brain interprets that as chaos. And this is the reason you can sit in a trendy, minimalist coffee shop for an hour and leave feeling weirdly exhausted and irritable, even if something bad happened. The space looked great, but it made your nervous system work overtime. And so the fix is to design for acoustic anchoring. You need to add in elements

not just because they look good, but because they absorb sound and stop that acoustic bounce. So start from the ground up. If you've got a rug and you've still got an echo in your room, drop a thick rug pad underneath it, because that pad often does more for sound absorption than the rug itself. Then soften your vertical surfaces. Use thick line drapery instead of relying only on blinds or shades. And when you choose art, prioritize pieces that don't add more hard reflection. So felt-backed art, tapestries, and unframed canvas are great choices. But framed glass prints can reflect sound almost as harshly as bare drywall. Because when you layer these soft sound-absorbing materials throughout your space, the entire room gets quieter in a really deep way. And

just like repositioning your furniture so your back isn't exposed to the room, that quieter sound profile signals safety to your nervous system. >> [music] >> But even if your room is quiet and comfortable, you can still wake up one day and hate how it looks. Because you might spend week in after week in nailing a specific aesthetic, but then a couple of months later you look at it and just feel nothing. >> [music] >> And it's not even that it looks bad. It's more that you feel weirdly disconnected from it. And most people blame that on being fickle or addicted to shopping. But a lot of the time, it's a psychological quirk known as the mere exposure effect. The mere exposure effect is the brain's tendency to prefer

things simply because they're familiar. It was first documented in the late 1960s by the psychologist Robert Zajonc, who noticed in his experiments that people rated random shapes and even nonsense words more positively after seeing them repeatedly. [music] And it's all because the brain equates familiarity with safety, and safety is good. But here's the problem with that.

Our brains didn't evolve in an environment where they could be shown the same aesthetic 300 [music] times in a single afternoon. And social media exploits that wiring at a scale the brain was never built to handle, manufacturing preferences you didn't actually choose. So contrary to what you might think, when you scroll Pinterest or Instagram for inspiration, you're [music] not seeing endless variety. You're actually seeing the same microtrends repeated in slightly different ways until they start to feel like your personality. The same arched mirrors, the same travertine table, and the same olive tree in the corner. And after your brain sees something 300 times, it starts to mistake exposure for taste. And because you now think you love these things, you build your living room around them. But that preference in

your mind is fragile, and the second the algorithm moves on, the spell breaks. And suddenly your room feels like it's not for you anymore. And that's where trend fatigue comes [music] from. So, how do you escape that cycle without swearing off inspiration completely? You need to run [music] an analog test. The point is to break the grip of the algorithm for long enough to figure out what you actually like when nobody is feeding [music] it to you. So, you step away from your phone and look at your real life. So, start with your closet. What colors do you wear repeatedly? Not the ones you bought for a fantasy version of yourself, but the ones you actually reach for. And look at the materials as well. Are you drawn to

crisp structured materials like leather and tailored cotton, or softer more lived-in textures like knitwear and denim? Then think about the places you love in the real world. That might be a hotel, a restaurant, or even a city you visited where you felt right at home. What did that place feel like? Was it warm and dim, bright and minimal, [music] old and layered? Lean into what makes you feel good. And then look at physical references. Go to your favorite bookstore or even a library and flip through architecture, interiors, and art books. Notice what catches your attention. This is different from just scrolling through social media feeds because books won't be in touch with today's algorithm, and they also aren't personalized to you. So, you'll catch yourself reacting to things before the

algorithm has had a chance to prime you. And when you anchor your design choices to your analog life like this, you bypass the mere exposure effect entirely. You stop designing to satisfy a feed and you start building a home that matches you. And that's the goal. Because a room built on your preferences will still feel like you 10 years from now, even after the internet has moved

on. But there's another layer to all this that most people never consider. Your home can match your identity perfectly and still leave you feeling drained. Because design isn't just about taste. It's also about energy. Because if you work in a modern office, commute into the concrete jungle, or live in a newly built apartment full of synthetic finishes, you probably feel pretty mentally wiped at the end of the day. And it's easy to blame that on your job or your poor sleep. But your environment has an outsized impact on your brain and it can either restore your attention or burn right through it. And this is where attention restoration theory comes in. Attention restoration theory was developed by a pair of environmental psychologists and the basic idea is that

attention isn't infinite [music] and it operates in two distinct modes. The first is directed attention, which I'll call effort mode. This is the type of attention you use when you're answering emails, reading spreadsheets, and driving in traffic. Your brain is constantly filtering, deciding, and blocking out noise. So it works hard, but it also burns out pretty quickly. >> [music] >> And then the second mode is soft fascination, which I'll call recovery mode. This is the type of attention you use when you watch tree leaves dance in the wind, stare at a campfire, or look at waves on the beach. These things hold your attention, but they don't demand anything from you. And that's why being in nature feels so restorative. Your brain gets to rest while still being

gently engaged. But here's the design mistake. We build homes that look sleek, but behave like an office. I'm talking perfectly smooth walls, flat cabinetry, plastic laminates, and fake wood. Everything machine-made, symmetrical, and flawless. But, when you sit in a room like that, your eyes have nowhere to land because there's no natural complexity, no visual softness, and no organic variation. So, your brain stays stuck in effort mode even when you're supposed to be off duty. And that's a recipe for low-grade, constant mental fatigue. So, the fix isn't just to add a plant. The fix is to bring in the kind of natural pattern your brain is built for. Because in nature, patterns are complex and irregular. Think about the grain in a piece of wood or the veins in

a natural stone. Your visual system evolved outdoors, so it processes that kind of pattern effortlessly. It's basically your brain's native language. So, when you introduce those kind of organic elements into your home, you give your attention a place to rest. The space stops demanding effort and starts offering recovery. So, if you want your home to recharge you instead of drain you, here are a few simple swaps that make a big difference. >> [music] >> First, start with your largest surfaces. Bring in real wood with visible grain rather than perfectly smooth painted finishes. And add in some natural stone if it fits your budget, even if it's just a small dose like a side table, a tray, or the base of a lamp. And look for veining and variation, not for

uniform patterns. Second, layer in natural textiles with some texture to them. So, think linen, wool, chunky cotton, and anything else with an irregular weave that catches light differently across the surface. And if you want the most budget-friendly version of this, focus on the things you touch and look at the most. Things like a wooden coffee table, linen curtains, or a ceramic lamp. Those are the kinds of places where soft fascination can have an instant impact. Because when your room has real natural complexity, your brain can stop working so hard, and that's when your home actually feels restorative. >> [music] >> But once your home stops draining you and starts restoring you, there's still something that can sabotage everything. And it's not your layout or your

lighting, it's the object you're keeping out of guilt. I mean, look around your room right now. Is there a piece of furniture you don't even like, but you refuse to get rid of? Maybe it's a massive armchair you spent a lot of money on years ago, or maybe it's carved dining table that you inherited from your parents that [music] completely clashes with the lighter, more modern look you want now. Whatever it is, odds are you're keeping it for reasons that sound responsible. It's [music] still in good condition, it was expensive when you bought it, or it has family history. But here's what's really happening. That one item is quietly dictating your entire room. It's forcing you to design around it, and it's costing you peace of

mind every time you enter the room. And so really, this comes down to two mental traps. The first is the endowment effect, which says that we overvalue things simply because we own them. In the moment something becomes ours, it feels more important than it actually is. And then the second is the sunk cost fallacy, which says that we hate letting

go of something when we've already invested money or emotion into it, even if it's making our life worse. And the result of these two traps is design paralysis, where you try to make that problem item work instead of admitting that it's a problem. And so you buy a new rug to distract from the chair, or you paint the walls to distract from the table, and you keep [music] spending money treating symptoms while the real issue stays firmly planted in the room. But here's the reframe that breaks that

spell. [music] I call it the stranger's price test. Stand in front of that piece of furniture that doesn't feel right to you, and imagine you don't own it. Instead, imagine you're in a thrift store or scrolling Facebook Marketplace >> [music] >> and you see that exact chair or table with a price tag on it. The question is, would you buy it right now and bring it into your home? Be honest with yourself here. If the answer is no, you wouldn't buy it today, then it's not a practical choice. It's psychological drag, and you have to think about it like this. The

money you spent years ago is already gone, and holding onto this piece of furniture doesn't get that money back. It just charges you a daily tax in the form of visual friction, guilt, and compromise. Because the fastest way to make your room feel lighter and more cohesive isn't buying 10 new decorative items. It's giving yourself permission to remove the high friction piece that you've been designing around for years. So, if you are holding onto that piece out of obligation, make a plan to sell it, donate it, or replace it. I promise you your future self will thank you. But once you remove that piece that's

been dragging your whole room down, the next step is making your space feel open again. And this next mistake is the one people most often make in small rooms. Because once you clear out the psychological dead weight, you need to place what's left in a way that doesn't trigger that cramped boxed-in feeling. But here's the problem. When a living room feels small or awkward, most people shove every piece of furniture tight against the walls because they think that by creating as much empty floor space as possible in the center, [music] that should equal a bigger room. But what you end up with is a living room with a layout that looks fit for a high school dance, and it makes the room feel cheaper and tighter, not bigger. Because

when furniture is flush against the wall, your eye loses its sense of depth. Everything turns into one flat outline around the perimeter, and the middle of the room feels like a dead void instead of usable space. This is the reason waiting rooms feel so weird. All the chairs line the walls and everyone stares into the empty center, but the rooms don't feel spacious. They just feel tense. But fortunately for you, the fix is actually simple, but it does take a bit of a leap of faith because you need to float the room. Now, I've talked about floating your furniture in a few different videos and I always get the same comment every time. That's great if you have a big living room, but what if

you live in a small apartment? And so I want to address that now. Because when I say float your furniture, you don't need to drag your sofa 2 ft away from the wall. You just [music] need to break the seal. So here's what you do. Pull your sofa 1 to 2 in or 3 to 5 cm off the wall. That's it. Because that tiny gap

[music] creates a shadow line behind the sofa and that shadow line is what tells your brain that the room has depth [music] and depth is what makes the room feel bigger. Now, that alone will make a surprisingly big difference, but if you want to take this a step further, there are two other things you can do as well. >> [music] >> First, make sure every room has one clear walking lane. So pick a single path from one side of the room to the other and keep that line clear. If you have to choose between a bigger coffee table and a clear walkway, choose the walkway every time. And if you're really tight on space, swap out bulky furniture pieces for more airy ones. So [music]

think a sofa perched up on feet, a chair with open arms, and a coffee table that allows air to pass under it. When you bring in those pieces, you're not just saving inches, you're also letting light pass through, which keeps the room feeling open and fresh. But now that you understand how your brain interprets your space, you're ready to take things to the next level. And that means learning a system to tie it all together. So watch this video next where I'll teach you one of the design frameworks I've developed for turning even the most basic, boring room into a space you love to spend time in.

So, don't be immediately alarmed by the high-pitched squeal the joints make when moving. There are two common types of gear reducers used in industrial robots. Small robots use harmonic drives, also called strain wave gear reducers. The one I have here is a brand new frameless harmonic drive. The ones in robots are usually a bigger integrated unit including bearings and seals to keep the grease in. This one is only the actual reducer. It's meant to be put in a machine to housing with bearings and seals added separately. They have a thin flexible inner spline and rigid outer spline that has two more

teeth than the inner one. Then a bearing fits snugly inside the flexible spline. Crucially, this bearing isn't a perfect circle. It's actually a slight ellipse, bending the flex spline so it meshes with the external spline at two sides. The input to the reducer is the center of that bearing. When it rotates, it moves where the splines are meshed together. The output is between the inner and outer splines, which would be connected to each side of the robot joint in this case. Since the outer spline has two more teeth than the inner spline, each time the input rotates one full rotation, the inner and outer spline move by two teeth as well, resulting in a total reduction between 50 to 200 to 1 typically. These reducers

don't always have a graceful failure where they slowly wear out, however. This robot has been through some sort of substantial crash. The J2 reducer is completely destroyed and the joint is free to move. The J3 reducer is still at least partially intact, but it's stiff to move and not at all smooth like it should be. After pulling it apart, it's clear this joint has also suffered a crash. The flex spline has started to twist and buckle in on itself. Those bumps in the flex spline aren't supposed to be there. It should be perfectly round like the new one. This kind of failure requires the reducer to be replaced. There's no repairing the flex spline. These were listed as parts robots like I mentioned before, so I

will eventually tear apart all of them and see what parts are good and what needs to be replaced, then build as many complete robots from the good parts as I can. The remaining good parts will either be used for other projects, kept as spares, or put on eBay to help fund future projects. The bigger robots don't just use giant harmonic drives. Instead, they use something called radial vector reducers, or RV reducers for short. I'm not going to take apart one of my big robots to show you a reducer, but luckily I got some brand new RV reducers as industrial surplus years ago and haven't used them for anything yet. This is a relatively big one. All of the joints on robots of this size typically

use RV reducers. My UP6 has small RV reducers on joints 1, 2, and 3 with the rest being small harmonic drives. I think harmonic drives are easier to manufacture once the joints need to be so small. I even have some insanely small ones about the size of a quarter. RV reducers have cycloidal discs surrounded by pins they mesh into with the count being off by one between them. Since the lobes are so much bigger than the teeth on the splines in harmonic drives, there aren't as many and the reduction ratio is lower. To help with this, there's an additional reduction between the motor and the cycloidal disc through standard spur gears that brings the reduction back to a similar range as harmonic drives. Now, don't be fooled

into thinking this is a planetary gear reduction. There is no outer ring gear that the larger spur gears are running against. Instead, they're attached to offset crankshafts that drive the cycloidal discs. This method of driving the discs from multiple points with much larger bearings is what separates RV reducers from plain cycloidal reducers, which are usually only driven from a single offset crank in the center. The pins on the outside are also able to rotate, which changes the bearing or wear surface from the small point where the cycloidal disc contacts the pin to the large cylindrical surface the pin is seated against, reducing friction and greatly improving the life of the reducer. The bearings supporting those crankshafts might seem oversized for handling the loads from those relatively

small input gears, and that's because they are. Those crankshafts and bearings are what carry the full output torque from the cycloidal discs to the joint the reducer is driving. There are There are cycloidal discs in this reducer. If you look past the top disc, you can see a second disc moving around underneath. Technically, only one disc would still work. The reason there are two discs is for balance and additional rigidity. A single disc would create quite a bit of vibration as it oscillates since it's off-center. The second disc is designed to move in the opposite direction as the first, so the vibrations cancel out.

This also means the loads on the crankshafts from the cycloidal discs are balanced. Each shaft is pushing the discs in opposite directions, and the discs mesh on opposite sides of the outer housing. That way the oscillating load from the discs mostly stays contained to the crankshafts, discs, and housing, rather than needing to go through all of the other bearings to keep the discs meshed with the outer pins. I'll eventually work on getting some of these other small robots up and running. Maybe make another video out of it. But first, I need to clear out space in the garage to work on the mobile robot arm. So, into storage they go. If you found this information helpful or want to keep up with my projects, be
sure to like and subscribe. Thanks for watching.

title: The Psychology of People Who Believe They Already Have What They Want

paragraphs.text: The psychology of people who believe they already have what they want begins with an act most people would call irrational. They act, feel, and decide as if the result existed [music] before there is any evidence. Most wait for confirmation before changing their identity. Those who believe they already possess what they want take that authority away from circumstances and refuse to let every delay, rejection, or difficulty decide who they are again. Neville Goddard called this >> [music] >> the creative power of imagination. In 1986, Hazel Markus and Paula Nurius offered a psychological parallel through

the concept of possible selves. This video explains how believing you already have what you want reorganizes attention, behavior, and persistence. Why your feared self uses the same force against you and how to change strategies without abandoning the identity you chose. If your identity waits for reality, it has already handed reality the command. >> [music] [music]

>> You already make decisions on behalf of a person who does not yet exist in the eyes of other people. >> [music] >> You can see it in the opportunity you avoid because you imagine you are not ready. In the conversation [music] where you lower your voice before anyone disagrees. And in the responsibility you accept before anyone recognizes you.

The future [music] may look distant on a calendar, but it enters your conduct whenever a possible version of you is given authority over a present choice. That authority works [music] in both directions. You can prepare for a position you do not yet hold treating competence and responsibility [music] as qualities of the person you have decided to become. You can also retreat from a rejection [music] that has not happened allowing a humiliated version of you to control the conversation before the other person responds. [music] In both cases, an anticipated identity is already organizing real behavior.

[music] Psychologists Hazel Markus and Paula Nurius called these versions possible selves. >> [music] >> They include who you might become, who you want to become, and who you fear becoming. A possible self is more than a goal. A goal describes something to reach, while an identity describes the person who will be present when that result arrives. It turns a general desire into a recognizable way of interpreting, >> [music] >> choosing, and responding. Consider the difference between wanting [music] respect and seeing yourself as someone worthy of respect. The desire can remain perfectly intact [music] while you accept constant interruption, present your ideas as apologies, and agree to conditions you believe are unfair. [music] Identity begins to change what you tolerate before recognition appears. The world has not confirmed the change,

yet it is already meeting behavior the old definition could not produce. This inner reference creates the confidence some people display before evidence. They were not secretly guaranteed that everything would work. They built a definition capable of guiding the present without asking circumstances for continuous permission. [music] The job does not exist yet, but a professional identity already [music] shapes their preparation. The relationship does not exist yet, but an emotionally mature identity already changes their boundaries. The financial result does not exist yet, but a responsible identity already decides what to do with the resources available now.

Circumstances keep their reality, but they lose the power to function as a complete definition. Being unemployed still means there is no job at this moment. [music] It does not mean competence disappeared along with the position. Loneliness remains a concrete condition, but it does not exhaust your capacity [music] to create intimacy. The balance in your account still requires honest decisions, yet it describes your current resources instead of decreeing [music] every future possibility. When these distinctions remain blurred, >> [music] >> every external fact enters identity directly. A negative response tells you that an attempt failed, but you convert it into a declaration of personal failure. A delay might reveal something about timing, >> [music] >> preparation, or strategy. The old definition turns it into proof that nothing will work.

You assign the event a function it does not possess, defining the person who will face the next situation. [music] When I encountered the idea of possible selves, I had to revisit decisions I had called prudent and admit that many of them were obeying a failure I had only imagined. I had decided on that failure in advance and then confirmed it through my own immobility. The feared future did not need to happen in order to exercise power. It was already participating in choices that could either prevent it or help produce it. Because fear already makes the future act on the present, you cannot honestly say you will live from a future identity only after receiving proof. The mind anticipates shame, abandonment, or defeat and rehearses their

consequences before any of them occurs. It brings a possible version into the present and begins arranging attention, posture, and behavior around it. The difference between those who believe they already possess the result and those who remain subordinate [music] to lack does not begin with the intensity of desire. title: The Art of Letting Go: Early Buddhist Teachings for Everyday Life

paragraphs.text: maybe you're like me when I was younger I craved attachment I had a very close relationship to somebody who broke my heart uh we had been dating for years we had even gotten made plans for the wedding and within a few days of the

wedding she backed out and it was of course devastating for me and this brought to mind I think directly the importance that attachment had for me and the way that attachment could lead to suffering in early Buddhism attachment is understood as one of the main causes of our suffering and that it stems directly from craving but there are ways of minimizing that suffering minimizing that attachment through a practice of Letting Go which is what

we'll talk about in today's video in one early suta the Buddha was asked what exactly is the purpose of living the spiritual life under the Buddha and his answer was the purpose of living the spiritual life under the Buddha is extinguishment by non-attachment in this video I'm going

to deal with some of the Practical aspects of dealing with attachment and how a practice of Letting Go can increase our mental well-being our relationships and indeed our overall happiness so this video will have six parts um six aspects here first we'll talk about attachment itself

why letting go of it is difficult third we'll talk about some practices of letting go then some benefits that those practices can give us some further practical tips and then I'll do a recap at the end first what is attachment now attachment is something that I think we

all naturally crave when we find something that makes us happy we naturally attach ourselves to it we cling to it we identify our ourselves with it we think of it as who we really are or some part of us in the sense that if we find happiness in material things a car maybe

some jewelry money that we attach ourselves to it we want those things more and more we find it difficult to give them up we can also attach to people to family to friends to workers co-workers we can even attach ourselves

to ideas and IDE s such as Freedom or country these abstract things that seem to make life so important for us in all cases however these things to which we attach ourselves are impermanent by their very nature and we tend to maintain unrealistic expectations of how these things will remain the same even as they change age and Decay this is perhaps most apparent

in physical things that surround us let's say a car when we first buy it shiny new but within a short period of time rust develops perhaps somebody dings it in the parking lot it Springs a leak somewhere the same can be true of people that we are attached to perhaps

they decide to have different interests their interests change over time and we tend to grow apart that's not something we'd planned and that's not something we had seen foreseen when we first met the person but inevitably perhaps it may happen with certain people in certain ways and if our growth does not coincide somebody who was a friend at

one point becomes a distant friend or we lose the friendship and even with ideas and ideals the concepts involved in them may change over time or from situation to situation what Freedom means means to us at one time maybe indeed completely different from what it means to us or to other people at a different time what a country is at one time may be different from another time our ideas and ideals may be coincident with people around us when we're young but then change as we grow older or the reverse so it's this constant change in the world and indeed

constant change in our self that brings suffering Buddhism talks about the Three Fires of greed hatred and delusion and greed or craving is the direct cause of this attachment which then brings suffering it brings suffering because
sometimes we cannot find those things to to attach ourselves to there's something that we want but we can't achieve want to attach but we can't find or we may have found it but now that we've found

it we have to expend effort energy stress worry on retaining it on keeping it the same so that it serves us the same function as it always has we have to maintain that car or that relationship or perhaps argue with somebody to try to bring them to our side so that we can maintain them in a certain way fitting into our lives or we may lose the thing we may lose our

sense of Freedom we may lose our sense of country we may lose a friend or a family member we may lose a possession and in all of those cases of course suffering follows second letting go of these attachments is difficult we seem

to be biologically wired to want to accumulate more and more stuff in order to feel safe and secure whether that stuff be material things that we can perhaps use at some time whether it be friends family other people around us that we can sort of accumulate put on our side all of these things make it seem as though the important part of life is to

accumulate more and more it may seem to us indeed that our safety and our very happiness depends upon this Contin accumulation now there's some truth to this having some things of course makes life easier and makes life safer and more secure and having friends and family can do the same but this attitude of continual accumulation and attachment

can be misapplied in ways that lead to our suffering basically our attachment to these things leads us to believe that we can control our lives through the possessions that we have through our attachments that our life our future is under our Direct Control and that if we let up our attachments if we begin to let go of our attachments our control will somehow slip out of our fingers but if we begin to look at that idea of control we can begin to see how it's an illusion because we really don't have

control over our lives in fact we don't even have true control over the things that we seem to possess and hold and that we're attached to that's the whole problem is that these things change under our very fingers in ways that lead to our suffering so if we can begin to see the problem of trying to control everything we can begin to see why

letting go is so difficult third we can turn to some practices of letting go and we can begin this idea of practices with some mental practices of Simply considering the idea of Letting Go what is the problem here what are the concerns we have if we begin to think of of holding on to the world like trying

to hold water in our hands we begin to see how gripping it more tightly simply makes it flow more quickly out that we cannot really grasp things that are fluid and flowing this growing awareness of how the world is fluid and how we

really cannot control that kind of change when we begin to see that we'll begin to relax around our ordinary tendency to grasp things and hold to them the same we'll find is true often with people that is the closer and

harder we grasp onto them the more that we push them away in this sense Letting Go doesn't mean isolating ourselves and it certainly doesn't mean pushing other people away from us what it means is allowing the other person to breathe in their own space we begin to learn the Deep truth that we cannot change another person unless they themselves want to change and even then change in a particular direction that is the same as
yours let's say or the way you would like may not be possible we begin to learn that true happiness our own true happiness does not depend upon our craving for the attachment with other

people but instead on a more open awareness that our happiness does not depend upon agreement with the attitudes and opinions of other people true deep caring depends upon our ability to hold the other person as they really are and not on expecting or requiring them to be as we want them to be another practice

that we might consider is to pursue a more minimalist lifestyle with our possessions the great uh architect Frank Lloyd Wright used to build houses that didn't have attics or a basements in in order to force people not to hoard and

and collect junk that they would stick in at attics and basements of course nowadays what we'll do is if we don't have an attic or a basement or enough space we'll go and rent a a storage unit somewhere and

Chuck stuff that we don't want into the storage unit and leave it until we're dead and then somebody else is going to crack open the storage unit and throw all the stuff out for us we know how life tends to work that way for us and

that's the kind of attitude that we perhaps should consider getting away from I've talked about how our house fire which some of you may have heard about I did some videos about it quite a while ago we had a house fire a few years years ago a couple years ago and although I did lose a few things that I'm sorry to have lost the the vast

title: My water heater is cooler than yours

paragraphs.text: Most of us don't think of water heaters very often. For all, they usually just... do their thing and the only time they cross your mind is when they stop doing their thing and you have a very unpleasant morning.

But water heaters are among the most energy intensive appliances in our lives. Though we take it for granted, Having hot water on demand is so energy intensive that a very ordinary water heater can cost upwards of 50 bucks a month to use.

But this water heater costs an average family less than $20 a month, and in the summer, using it is arguably free. How on Earth could that be? Because this machine heats the water inside the tank by chilling the air surrounding it. This is a heat pump water heater.

Quite literally the coolest kind of water heater you can buy. Traditionally, to heat water we have had to import heat energy from an external source, either the power grid or some sort of heating fuel like natural gas or propane.

This water heater, on the other hand, uses the same technology as your refrigerator - but in reverse. Your fridge works by pulling heat out of its interior and throwing that heat outside, which is why your fridge gets warm as it runs. But this thing gets cold as it runs because it does exactly the opposite. It collects heat from the air around it and bottles it up inside. This may seem like a strange way to heat water,

but relocating heat which is already there requires just a fraction of the electricity that releasing new heat with an electric heating element does. As in as little as one fourth as much electricity. And this is not just any heat pump water heater.

it to resistive mode won't happen until the future. And even then, I probably still won't do it.

well, then you've pretty much defeated the point of using the heat pump. than a resistive heater would release using the same amount of electrical energy. So if my home is heated with a heat pump and that heat ends up getting gobbled up by the water heater, it may seem a bit silly, but it's perfectly rational.

as is the case inside the refrigeration circuit, the pressure of that refrigerant tells you its literal temperature and vice versa. And as temperature goes up, so does pressure. This means that as the water in the tank warms up,

refrigerant pressure on the high side slowly climbs, which makes the compressor work harder and harder. And we can see this in the power draw. until hitting a max of roughly 460W. That's a pretty huge difference. But so is the pressure difference. At 120 degrees, R-513a condenses at 180 psi - three times the pressure. But because the refrigerant needs to actually be hotter than the water to heat it,

it was probably condensing around 135°F, which would be a pressure of 220 psi. That's why it's working so much harder and drawing more power. When set to the factory default of 120°F, it would essentially always stop at 460W of power draw.

But when I bumped the set point up to 130 Fahrenheit, it would climb all the way to 500W. This is the highest temperature I would ever set it to for efficiency’s sake. But what's interesting
is every time you draw a hot water out of the tank

and some cold water enters at the bottom, refrigerant pressures immediately fall and so power draw does, too. Here I was doing laundry and set the washing machine to hot. Normally I don't do that because modern laundry detergents work great in cold water.

It's fine. But the other interesting thing about the condensing temperature of the refrigerant is that we can look at the power draw to get a sense of the average water temperature inside the tank. For example, here, power draw began around 400W since it was just replenishing

And while I don't know if they all work like this with a full tank of hot water, it ignores small draws. Even if I take a 20 minute shower, it usually doesn't react to that.

Unless you draw some minimum volume of water out of it in one go, which I'm estimating to be between 15 and 20 gallons, it will effectively just sit there and wait until the top portion of the tank has cooled off enough to justify starting back up. I'm guessing this was done by moving

the bottom temperature sensor a good way up the tank, and that it was done specifically for humidifiers. My old water heater, and indeed every other I've ever paid attention to, would fire up almost immediately after you start using hot water.

In fact,
it would start up twice during the course of a dishwasher cycle, which probably uses six gallons tops. And so the old water heater would typically respond to the humidifier after it had been running for 15 minutes or so.

But as far as I can tell, this water heater has never responded to the humidifier. It might run just a bit longer the next time it fires up,
but it'll make it all day before that happens unless I use hot water in some other way so I can happily report
that all winter there was never a problem. This room did get dryer whenever it finally decided to start, but the rest of the house stayed delightfully moist. But speaking of the rest of the house,

let's finish up with all this nonsense. It is true that my HVAC system’s one and only air intake is in this room, but the shape of this room causes much of the air discharged by the water heater to be trapped.

Virtually no airflow moves across the room because the supply register, which provides heating and cooling from the furnace, is on the same side of it as the air intake, and thus it creates this massive dead zone.

And the utility closet is in that dead zone. So when the water heater runs, pulls in air from over here and discharges it into the closet, once that cold air seeps out, the furnace isn't actually grabbing all that much of it. This means, especially in the spring,

this room did start to get kinda chilly at times. And because I'm me, I solved that problem with a bathroom fan, a temperature controller, and a second thermostat. So that bathroom fan mounted to the wall pulls
air from the back corner of the closet, which is right near the water heater’s exhaust vent, and blows it through this duct to push it out of the closet right above my furnace’s air intake.

fan come on at the same time. Now, regardless of whether my thermostat
is requesting heating or cooling, when the water heater starts running, the furnace fan and the bathroom fan will help move the cold air from inside the closet. Get the furnace to suck it up and spread it around my home. Now this works and it works decently well,

another six inch duct to the water heater, especially since it has to get behind the water pipes

This temperature controller solution works, but not all that well.

In fact, it's not working much at all in the warmer weather because it usually doesn't get colder than 57 degrees in the closet. And I need to adjust the set point. So I'd rather just have some way to turn on the fan whenever the water heater is on
which an auxiliary power outlet would let me do. I'd also like to see an auxiliary relay, so you can send a fan call to an HVAC system at the same time without hooking up a second thermostat.
But you know, I've got stuff and I know how to use it. But I was caught off guard by how loud that bathroom fan would be, and it's not actually because of the fan.

I deliberately got a very quiet one. It's mostly because of this vent. Since this awful bathroom fan situation ended up making more noise than I expected, and since actually getting it to work well would require fiddling with the set point throughout the year,

I am going to try and run another six inch duct to the water heater’s exhaust collar and put a larger and more normal kind of vent where this one is. After doing that, in theory, I can remove the intake duct

and put that vent back to code compliance status. Once I do this, the water heater itself will solve the dead zone problem in this room, and since its discharge air will still be right above the furnace intake distribution throughout my home should be the same as now.
I am mildly worried that an exhaust duct might sweat with condensation in the warmer and more humid parts of the year, but this room does get pretty dry after it's been running for a while,

and it always runs for at least two hours at a time, so I'm not sure whether that will actually be an issue. I’ll pin a comment if it does. And, well I'll also have to play around with new solutions for forcing the furnace fan to come on.

I'm thinking what I'll probably do is just move that thermostat outside the closet and right next to the discharge vent. It's a dumb solution, but I tend to prefer those, and it'll make adjusting the temperature at which the furnace fan kicks on throughout the year trivial, while also giving me the option to disable that outright. And... that's about it.
But I do have a loose end to tie up. That video I mentioned on electric water heaters? At the end of that one, I told you about a mystery box I threw together, which would allow me to disable

the water heater when electricity prices are high. I'm on variable electricity rates because I'm a sicko who likes to game that sort of thing. title: The Greatest Rebrand in History: Addison Rae

to be perfectly honest, I was just a little lazy. So, today, we're back with a new video for the start of the new school year, to get back into learning French. And today, I thought, why not try

a new concept where I'll show you memes about France? In French, we say "même," maybe it's the same in English. I don't know, but I'm going to show you memes about France and try to give you my perspective as a French person on these memes, to see if what we see on social media,
if the memes we see on social media, are true or not. So I've selected a few memes, and we'll go through them one by one. I'm going to give you the video chapters for each meme

, and I'll show you the memes on screen as well, of course. And we'll start with the first one: "When people think you eat snails and frogs because you're French." What ? This meme is half true, I think. So it's true that often when we say

we're French, people think, "Oh, but you eat snails , snails, and frogs! " And to tell you the truth, to the point that, for example, the English call us "Froggies," we call the English "Rosbifs," and they
call us "Froggies." So this idea that we eat a lot of frogs and snails is a very widespread cliché, but it's something that's half true. Simply because I think eating snails isn't common, but

I think it's easy to find in France. If you go to a typical bistro, for example in Paris, you have restaurants called "bouillons." In different neighborhoods, there's a "bouillon," which is a typical restaurant and not very expensive.
Normally, on the menu, you can choose snails, often snails. Well, I tried it once, and because it didn't really appeal to me, I don't really want to eat snails, and in fact, it's not

, how can I say, I don't find it very interesting because there are the snails , and then they put butter and garlic on top , and this butter and garlic sauce is what gives it the flavor. So when you eat snails, you mostly get the impression of eating butter and garlic.
And the texture is a bit strange. So, for example, as a Frenchman, I don't eat snails and I don't eat frogs, so that's why it's a cliché, a generalization. In the case of snails,

yes, you can find them on a menu in a French restaurant, that's possible. Are they good? Personally, I'm not a fan, but butter with garlic is generally very good, but the texture is a bit unusual. As for frogs,

I find that a bit stranger because the only times I've had the opportunity to eat frog legs— and a leg is the upper part of the leg— generally, we eat frog legs. Well, the only time I had the opportunity to eat

frog legs was in a Chinese restaurant, I think, an Asian restaurant, but I believe it was Chinese. And that's what's a bit strange, there's this cliché that the French eat frogs. But if you want to find frog legs,

I'd almost recommend going to a Chinese restaurant. And I don't know if it's something typically Chinese or if Chinese restaurants in France thought, " Let's please the French and put frogs on the menu." But in any case, typically, in bistros, in

restaurants, for example, bouillons, you don't find frogs. I've never seen them on a menu. And that 's why I said it's half true; snails, yes, why not, but frogs, you can find those, but not in typical French restaurants, I think. So there you have it, that's a bit of a cliché.

I think it's also because these are countries where there's a good level of English. , France, please don't! I wanted to talk about this meme because there's this cliché that... If you try to speak French with French people, they'll get annoyed. They'll tell you not to try to speak French if you don't know how to speak French.

First, there's a distinction to be made between Paris and the rest of France. This distinction is important because I think reactions can be very different from one place to another. In France, and especially between Paris and, for example, a town in the countryside. The reason

is quite simple: Paris is the most touristy city in the world. So, when French people living in Paris see a foreigner, they aren't surprised; they just think, "Okay." For example, people who work in very touristy places often

experience pressure, there are a lot of people, they don't have time, they're in a hurry, and so, if you try to speak French, they'll say, "Yes, what do you want?" And I think that's typical of Paris , and it's typical of all capital cities in the world— this "I don't have time, I'm in a hurry" attitude. When I was in Japan, in Tokyo, because

there are so many foreigners and tourists, people aren't particularly curious if you go to the Japanese countryside. Well, when I went to the Japanese countryside, people were curious and asked us, "What are you doing here?" Plus, people didn't speak English, etc. And I think it's the same in France.

If you go to the French countryside and you meet French people, they'll be surprised, they'll ask you questions, and often they don't speak English, so they'll speak to you in French. So that's the first difference. And then I think there's a more cultural aspect , or for example,

if I take Asian cultures, I think it's very different. Cultures of French or European culture, I mean in the way of being. But if we take, for example, the United States, which is culturally closer, I'm thinking of the United States, there's always this thing where

every sentence 100%. If that were the case, you'd already be fluent and you wouldn't have to learn French anymore. So, this part of trying to guess, but I'm not sure, and maybe I'm taking a risk by answering something.

exactly what the person meant. For example, I'm going to show you an... I'm going to give you an example of a misunderstanding. When I was in Japan, I worked on a farm , and the family had fish in a bowl. So, a bowl is a container

with water for fish, a fishbowl, for example, goldfish . So there were fish in a bowl. And one evening, I wanted to ask, "Have the fish ever eaten?" I tried to ask this question in Japanese , and the person looked at me a bit strangely

and said, "No, we don't eat fish." And I was like, " No, no, it's a misunderstanding, it's a misunderstanding. Sorry, I didn't mean that. I meant to ask, 'Have they ever eaten? Have they ever eaten?' So, that's a misunderstanding, and I think you have to accept that risk because it's perfectly natural." So when someone speaks to you in

very fast French, don't give up, try to understand. And if you only understand a few words, try to guess the meaning. And then, of course, you'll have situations like this meme where someone speaks to you in
very fast French and you'll think, "Wow!" Yes, yes. And personally, I had the exact same experiences in Japan, and I think it's perfectly natural. For the next one, I chose a slightly political meme.

So this is a meme that I think the French will appreciate, and it's a meme that deals a bit with misunderstandings. So, in the photo on the left, it's a meme template, a very popular meme format taken from the Star Wars movies.

So these are photos , images taken from the Star Wars films. And actually, that's it, there are four boxes , and in the first box is Emmanuel Macron, the President of the French Republic, the French president, saying, "I'm going to eradicate the poor." Then, I can't remember his name.

I'm not a big Star Wars fan, but I can't remember that name. Anyway, it's Natalie Portman, right? Anyway, she says, "You mean poverty? You mean I'm going to eradicate poverty?" Emmanuel Macron doesn't answer and says, "

You mean poverty, is that it? No, there." So in France, Emmanuel Macron isn't popular. He's been President of the Republic for two terms , and there are all the problems that are quite common in Western societies recently,

meaning that purchasing power is decreasing, people are getting poorer, and the price of gas is going up, the price of everything is going up, there's inflation, etc., etc. So overall, Emmanuel Macron isn't popular.

And it's often said that he's a bit of a "president of the rich." So these are very French political issues. But here, the amusing misunderstanding— it's a bit cynical, but amusing—is that he says "I'm going to eradicate the poor" instead of "I'm going to eradicate poverty."

Normally, a president of the Republic, to get elected, would say "I want to eradicate poverty." To eradicate means to eliminate completely; I want to eliminate poverty, I don't want there to be any more poor people in France.

But here, he says "I'm going to eradicate the poor." That's the kind of misunderstanding you can make in French. If you say "I'm going to eradicate the poor," people will look at you like, "Wow! You seem a bit extreme." Whereas if you say, "I'd like to eradicate poverty," people will think, "Wow,

that's really a good person, they have good qualities, good values," and so on. So, that was mainly to show you an example of a possible misunderstanding. And to give a little introduction to French politics

, we have the second-to-last meme: Grandma invited us over on Sunday at noon, Grandma on Sunday evening. These are images taken from the film Spirited Away, which is a very popular Japanese film, and I think it's common

to all grandmothers, to all grannies around the world. But often, when you go to eat at Grandma's in France, there's a lot of food. And typically, the typical phrase from a French grandmother is that when you've finished your plate,

when you've finished eating, she'll say, " Oh, would you like some more food? Would you like to eat something else?" Then you say, "No, I can't take it anymore, I'm so full, I can't eat anything, I can't swallow anything."

to go on Sundays at noon, and often these meals last a very long time. Often we start, we sit down at the table— we say "se mettre à table," meaning we start the meal around noon—and often it lasts until 4 or 5 p.m.

in the world is Lofi Girl, so that's the one you see at the top. And actually, the interesting thing, I think, is that the background represents the city of Lyon. The city of Lyon in France for two reasons. Well, mainly for one reason.

the view of the city of Lyon, and that's what inspired him. Regarding the young girl who was studying, the video originally used a clip from a Japanese film by the same director as Spirited Away,
called Whisper of the Heart. It's a film I really love, and in it, there's a scene where the young girl, the heroine, the main character, is studying at her desk. Initially, the channel used

this image. They couldn't use it anymore because it's copyrighted. So, they asked someone to create an animation. The person who did the animation lived in Lyon. Now, I don't know for sure , and that's why the Lofi girl is French and the setting represents a French city.

That's all for today. I hope you enjoyed this new format. I think it's interesting because it's kind of funny, kind of silly, these memes , and at the same time there's always a bit of a cultural aspect behind them. It allows me to talk about different topics in a single

video, so I think it's interesting. If you liked it, feel free to let me know in the comments. If you have any memes about France that you like, feel free to send them to me on Instagram. And if you enjoyed this, I'll make more videos like this one.
Thanks for watching until the end , and I'll see you next time.

title: Let's Help This 83-Year-Old for FREE!

paragraphs.text: Hi, welcome to Midwest Magic Cleaning. My name is Buff Stuffalophagus and this week we're helping an 83-year-old man who's under such a severe pile of junk that he hasn't been able to access his hobbies for at least 5 years. His granddaughter has been trying to help him out for at least 4 and 1/2 years, but this is a big job and not only is it a big job, but it's a it's an expensive job because you have to be able to pay for a dumpster and those are not cheap. Fortunately, because you guys watch the channel and you subscribe to the channel, we're able to afford that dumpster and we have the knowledge and the resources to do this in a couple of hours. Now, the reason I think this one

is so special is because, like I said, he's 83 years old. He doesn't have a lot of mobility, but the things that he likes to do are in the garage. He likes to tinker with tools and build stuff and work on wood projects. There's also a bunch of fishing poles in here, so I know he liked to fish at one point, but it was impossible to access, especially for somebody who doesn't have a lot of mobility. I had trouble accessing it and I I walk just fine. So, it brought me a lot of pride to be able to get in here and free up a bunch of room so that he could access the fishing poles or if he wanted to just sort his tools or work on

something, you know, woodworking, he can actually get in here and do that. As a guy who likes to tinker, I know that if you took all that stuff away from me, I would go nuts over time. I have to be doing something. And so, especially when you're at that age, boredom sets in pretty easy and it means a lot to me that he is able to get out here and do

the things that he loves to do. Plus, there's really one important thing that I don't think people from cities may understand as much as people like me who live in a really rural country area. So, we're just corn and soybeans and cows
and pigs. Like, that's that's all we are here in Southern Illinois. It It takes Just to get to an interstate, it takes me a 30-mi drive. And they're very small towns with nothing to do. There's

something so peaceful about having, say, a thunderstorm rolls in, and it's not a dangerous one, but you can just sit underneath your carport or in the garage with the garage door open and watch it storm. It's a thing we like to do, and it's so peaceful, and it's so relaxing, and just allowing him to get out of here and grab a chair and watch it rain. To me, that means something, and I think to him it means something as well. So, if all we accomplish by clearing out this garage is just to give him space to sit and relax, to me, that's worth it. Now, even if you can't relate to that, there is one thing that I think most of you can relate to, which is the garage is

typically, in, say, a logic form, one of the best places to store items because it's out of the way, it's not in your house, there's usually plenty of room in a garage, but in practice, it's the worst place you can store anything. And the reason is because most garages aren't heated and cooled, and even if they're waterproofed, you know, from a a roof standpoint or from an insulation standpoint, they collect a lot of humidity. And so, tools are going to rust, spray paint cans are going to rust, any furniture that you have there is going to take on water and get water and mold damage. Chairs that have fabric on them are definitely going to get mold, same thing with mattresses. They're going to get dirty and moldy and

just gross and unusable over time. Not to mention the infestation of spiders that is 100% guaranteed to happen in a garage. We did a house earlier this year that had a a couple of sewing machines that were foot-pedaled, so they weren't electric, they were just operated by just swinging your feet on a grate underneath it, and that would have been in the late 1800s or early 1900s. They didn't have room in the house to store

it, so they stored it in a garage and it utterly 100% destroyed both of those antiques. The metal was rusted beyond repair, but even if they could repair the metal, the wood had been so damaged from mold and water damage that there was no saving it. The wood had warped beyond repair. So, those beautiful pieces of history that they wanted to save ended up completely destroyed because they didn't know how to properly store it. They just put it in the in the garage and thought that'll be fine, and it wasn't. So, if you have no choice but to store some things in a garage, what I would suggest would be to completely encapsulate anything that's fabric like a mattress or a love seat or whatever in

plastic and make sure it's 100% sealed on all sides. And if it's wood or cardboard, it needs to be off the floor. Put it on a pallet or put it on something that it doesn't let it contact the floor because cardboard will completely disintegrate and wood acts like a sponge for any moisture, not just standing water, but humidity. If you have things that can be put in tubs, don't get the cheap tubs. Get something that it has an an airtight seal on it. Spring for the extra because if not, everything you put in there is going to eventually get damaged. I would suggest not storing many things in your garage. So, my rule of thumb for my own garage would be lawn care stuff, tools, and

then seasonal decorations, and that's about it. If I find myself packing clothes for another season, there's a good chance I'm never wearing those clothes again. And so, all I'm doing by storing those things is delaying a decision. And that decision would be to get rid of them. I know eventually I'm going to do it, but all I'm doing is putting off that decision and making it highly unlikely that I'm ever going to go out there and actually get rid of them until it's so out of control that I'm forced to do it and now I made so much more work for myself. >> [snorts]

>> If you're saving things that you're wanting to pass down to your family when you pass, I would first find out if your family even wants that stuff before you start storing them in a garage. Because one, storing them in a garage is not a good place to store them. There's a good chance you're going to damage whatever it is that you're passing down to your family. And two, look up a channel, I think they're on Tik Tok and Instagram called Millennial Inheritance. I think that's ran by a guy named Nick Fox and they kind of poke fun at the things that their parents had left for the kids that are just collections of the weirdest just piles of junk you can imagine. Avon bottles that are absolutely worthless,

magazines, China sets that are so gaudy and so worthless. They meant something to the parents, but they mean absolutely nothing to the kids. If the kids look at that and say, "No, I'm not interested in that. I I appreciate the thought, but that is not for me." Don't store all this extra crap in your garage because you're just taking up space. What they're actually inheriting is a very large trash bill after you pass because now they've got to rent a dumpster and

then put in all the elbow grease in order to get rid of all that stuff that you thought was cool. I have cleaned out so many houses of somebody who's passed away and their kids just don't want to go through the physical and mental anguish of cleaning those out and in every single case that I've ever done, the kids only want photo albums. If they have a few things in there that have monetary value, they will always say, "We can maybe sell that on eBay or find a family member who wants it, but I'm not concerned about any of that other stuff, just the photo albums." The only other things that I've seen them keep have been maybe some games that they had when they were a kid that the parents

never got rid of and that was just for nostalgia sake. It had no connection to their parents at all. I would say in most cases that if the house isn't clean enough and in good enough repair to have an estate sale, only keep maybe five things that you're wanting to hand down to kids because so far in every case I've ever done, I may get rid of say five full-size dumpsters of stuff from a house and the kids may keep five things out of all that stuff total. And the

things that they keep are typically something that's so small they can just put in one back seat of their car. The reason that I mentioned that in this particular video is because they had told me when I first started that there were several boxes by the door that they wanted to save because it was stuff for the family. And we did save it. It was totally fine, but it was like two Rubbermaid tubs full of Avon bottles and then several boxes that just had a bunch of candles and stuff. Now, I I'm not saying that the kids don't want that stuff. Maybe they do. But at first glance it seems like out of your whole life, you spent 83 years on this Earth, and then the things that you're really

adamant about handing down are things that in 99% of the cases the kids could not care less about. They don't care about the candles. They don't care about Avon bottles from the 1970s. It seems like there could be more sentimental things that you can hand down than that. Again, they may love it. They may be like, I definitely want those Avon bottles when you pass. But it's worth having a conversation about before you start storing all that stuff. You can also look at it this way. Your grandma invites you over and says, "I'm getting rid of all my possessions tomorrow. You can take whatever you want from this house." If she brought the whole family in there and told them that, there's a high likelihood that the only things

they would walk out with are practical things. Like, "I'd really like that TV. Oh, you've got a nice KitchenAid mixer. I could use that." They're probably not walking out with some painting that she's had since 1960. They're probably not going to look in the kitchen and say, "Oh, I've always loved that China cabinet. Let me have that." That's not saying that that those things don't exist. There are plenty of people who have really nice furniture that would make beautiful heirlooms and they're worth handing down, but I'm saying for the most part and in the the dozens and dozens of cases that I've personally worked on, they've never wanted any of that stuff. They've wanted the practical things that they can use in their everyday life. And I can tell you with

100% certainty that none of those things came out of a garage. I've never met a kid or an adult yet who has been like, "Oh, those storage units where you put all that stuff that wasn't good enough for your own home? I want that stuff." But especially the things that you collect, if your kids don't also collect them, they're not interested in them. They don't want your 57 piece matching set of moose-shaped cookie cutters. You

care about the coffee mugs that you collected from each state because you put time and effort and energy into it. What they see when you pass is now they have to carry this big-ass heavy box of 50 coffee mugs to the garbage. So, where this garage is concerned is they gave us a criteria. Keep any toys that aren't broken, get rid of everything that is broken or damaged or dirty beyond repair. We will keep the tools and everything else can go. So, we went a step beyond that and we saved things like Christmas trees and Halloween decorations because they were neatly put into Rubbermaid tubs. They were protected, they were clean. And now when those seasons roll around, they can just pull those off the shelf and there they

go. We kept the old fishing poles, but we put them all together. Um all the extra chairs that they had, we put those all together. So, if they have a family reunion or or whatever, a break-dance battle, they've got enough chairs for people to pull up a seat and watch and judge. All the tools went together. All the spray paint cans went together, even though technically I should have gotten rid of those because they were all rusted. But also, there are rules with dumpsters. You can't throw a bunch of aerosol stuff in there. Anyway, that's a whole 'nother story. But we at least got those off the floor and into a dry plastic tub to where they weren't contacting wet concrete anymore. There's one thing I didn't do in here and I'm

glad I didn't. I did not organize his tools and one of the reasons that I didn't do that was because well, two reasons. One, I was exhausted by the time we got done with this, but two, I think he's going to enjoy doing that himself. I think that he's so into those hobbies that now that he has the room to actually get out here in the garage, it's going to be a fun thing for him to separate all of his wrenches and put them back in their correct drawers and set all of his oil cans over to the side and just organize. Every guy that I know typically just everything starts out organized, then as you get more and more projects, you get a little less

organized, so you start throwing wrenches just on the workbench and then there's a point where you look around and go, "Okay, this is out of control. Let me stop and organize all this and put things back where they go." And every dude that I know, once he finishes those, he he's proud of it. He wants to open the drawers and show his wife and say, "Hey, check all this out, huh? Huh?" And I'm not saying that women don't like doing that. It's just I've only known men who, you know, have a bunch of tools in the garage and tinker and all that. So, the point is I left that because I think it would be a fun project for him to do because I can see

by the way he's got his garage set up that he was very particular about where he put things at one point. It just got so cluttered and so trashed out that eventually he couldn't get back there to do it and it was just so overwhelming. It was like, "What's the point?" >> If you're new to this channel, we do all

of our cleanings for free, every single one of them, including the dumpsters. We end up buying the dumpsters for the people who we help, unless they're a landlord or an investor or something like that, which I tend to stay away from, but occasionally we'll do videos like that. The reason we can do that and the reason we can afford it is because people watch the videos and they hit the subscribe button. The subscribe button doesn't cost anything. It's a free thing. It just lets YouTube know, "Hey, I like this channel and I like these videos. I'd like to see more stuff like this." So, if you haven't hit the subscribe button, please do because we're nearing a million subscribers right now and that's a huge goal that

I've set myself and it's been about 4 years and we're so close to hitting it now. Every click of that subscribe button really, really helps. Again, doesn't cost you anything. It just helps us out. The other thing that helps us afford this is that I have an online store called midwestmagiccleaning.com where I sell professional and specialized cleaning rags. I also sell funny t-shirts and coffee mugs and all kinds of stuff that I think you'd really like. Again, that's midwestmagiccleaning.com and I don't sell anything on that site that I don't personally use myself in my own cleanings as well as the cleanings that you see on these videos. All that being said, members, I will see you on Wednesday. Everybody else, I'll see you next weekend. Later.
