title: No Money? Here’s How You Escape the Permanent Underclass

paragraphs.text: Hello world. I'm an unemployed ex big tech software engineer with 25 years of experience in the tech industry. So, involuntary early retirement has given me a lot of time to think. And one of the things that I think about a lot is this idea of escaping the permanent underclass. So, to give some context, America is becoming a K-shaped society

where the top leg of the K represents people who own assets. Think assets like financial investments. The bottom, vastly larger leg of the K represents people who don't own capital. People who must survive based on the wages of their labor. Now, the theory here is that over time, the value of that capital it should grow exponentially. The idea

being that capital ownership of things like AI, robotics, and automation it should over time do more and more the work required to keep society running. Whereas the value of labor, it would gradually decrease over time, right? As a person's mind and body gradually ages

and degrades over time. Now, it's possible that this gap becomes unbearable and at some point we get a revolution. The game board gets turned upside down and everyone can start off equal again. It's a real possibility. But as I've discussed in past vlogs, it's also possible that the two legs of the K will grow wider and wider over time until social mobility becomes impossible. And that massive bottom leg will eventually transform into a

permanent underclass. And the entire society would become a kind of techno-feudalism where you will own nothing and be sad. Now, if we look at societies throughout history, feudalism is actually pretty common. And in fact, it may be a more stable social system than our own current system. So, bottom line, barring a major social transformation or a violent revolution, most people will enter the permanent underclass. Possibly in as short of a timeline as 5 to 10 years. And the most realistic way to escape this permanent

underclass is to gain financial independence. That is, you must gain ownership of financial assets that would allow you to survive without having a job. But, how do you gain financial independence within this 5 to 10 year timeline when you have little or no money to begin with? What if you're in debt with a negative net worth? So, I have spent some time thinking about this and I got some advice to share. So, let's jump in. Now, a lot of people,

they view the journey of achieving financial independence kind of like stumbling upon an easy money miracle. Usually, this is something like getting in on the ground floor of an insanely speculative investment, like an NFT that promises insane returns, something like 1,000% return per year, or something like stumbling upon an easy source of

passive income, where you could work 4 hours per week on a laptop on a beach somewhere and make $1 million a year, or building an AI-powered business where the AI does all the work and you're pulling 100K monthly reoccurring revenue while you sleep. I'm going to tell you

guys all right now that this is all a fantasy. A fantasy sold by countless numbers of financial influencers and internet gurus. Passive income is rarely truly passive. Like, if you publish a $20 ebook, it won't automatically make you rich. AI won't magically automate a

business into profitability. And speculating on those NFTs, man, that's just gambling with extra steps added in. So, you got to stop believing in the myth of easy money. Becoming financially independent for the vast majority of people in this world is a difficult and long-term undertaking. Now, if you're starting from $0, it is critical that you build a base of financial stability before even thinking about financial independence. And achieving this stability requires that you embrace frugality. This involves taking a hard look at your expenses, your income, and your debt to understand your true starting point. It involves understanding which of your expenses are essentials, things like housing, food, utilities, and which expenses are

optional. Now, [snorts] being frugal, it's a pretty broad concept. Some people are totally comfortable with insanely tight budgets. Imagine cutting all non-essential spending, things like subscriptions, eating out, consumer goods, maybe even heat and meat consumption. Some people can be perfectly fine with this extreme level of frugality. For other people, some creature comforts are actually essential, and they cannot cut down their budgets the absolute minimum. And even for the same person, a person's relative level of frugality, it could actually shift and [snorts] change over time. So, it's up to the individual to find their own threshold for sustainable

frugality. With frugality, you're living below your means. You're spending less than you earn, and you're pocketing the difference as savings. With the savings, you can build an emergency fund, something like 3 to six months of essential living expenses. So, an unexpected event doesn't completely upend your life. You can pay down and eventually pay off your debts. And eventually, you'll be able to redirect these surplus savings towards safe and sustainable investments. Now, one way to accelerate your journey to financial independence is to create actual value. The basic formula here is simple. Find a

real difficult problem. Become good at solving that problem. Help other people and get paid for the value that you create. This requires mastering the skills that allow you to solve these hard problems. Skills for whatever these problems are, right? Like, for example, engineering skills to make things, marketing skills for getting attention, sales skills for closing the deal and monetizing, management skills for project execution, and so on. With focused effort, most people can achieve mastery in a specific skill within a pretty reasonable amount of time. Like, less than a thousand days. Being able to solve these harder problems allows you to get higher income. Now, you can get this higher income via working for somebody else, like in a day job, or by working for yourself. In my opinion,

it's a good idea to have an income engine that you control entirely. Build a business that you own, rather than entirely relying upon a job to get money. The goal here is to create something that can eventually make you money without directly consuming your labor. Now, I have discussed in detail on a past vlog about all the opportunities that are presented by the age of AI. But, the bottom line here is that today's technology, it allows us to create businesses and reach potential customers much faster than in past eras. To create value, you don't necessarily

need permission from gatekeepers or a prestigious degree or even decades of experience. And here's the thing, time waits for no man. It's easy to sit there and just consume content. You might even have some clever ideas. But without action, it's just not enough. Remember, we may have only 5 to 10 years before the window of

opportunity is permanently closed. So, you need to stop consuming content. Stop endlessly preparing. Stop making excuses and start doing. You need to get out there and solve the problems that people actually care about solving. Now, once you got some money coming in, it makes sense to make that money work for you. Because after all, we live in a hyper-capitalist system. What does that mean? It means to take your savings and invest it in assets that has a high

probability of preserving its value and a high probability of delivering a good return. Now, speaking of investment, sometimes it's necessary to use leverage, also known as debt, to invest in highly productive assets. In my opinion, it's very important to distinguish between good debt and bad debt. An example of good debt would be like using debt to buy assets or to grow a business. One where there's a super

high probability of that asset delivering a good return while preserving its value. Bad debt is when you take on debt to get things that has a low to zero probability of delivering a good return. Things that may actually depreciate in value. Think status symbols, lifestyle, man toys, and so on. As a rule, you should never spend money

on things that don't generate future returns. Now, I'm not a financial advisor. I'm just speaking from my own personal experiences, so you should take it with a massive grain of salt. But for me, ownership of certain assets like rental real estate near major urban

centers or large diversified index funds or ownership of businesses that I know very, very well, businesses where I have an asymmetric advantage. These asset classes seem to have done very well for me over long periods of time. So, net-net, financial independence doesn't come from finding some sort of magical easy money hack. For the vast majority of people, there is no easy silver bullet. It comes down to living below your means, solving valuable problems that other people are willing to pay for, and then putting that money to work where it can generate for you more money. And I truly believe that if even some of the people listening to this puts these principles into action, they can build real financial independence, gain control over their lives, and escape the

permanent underclass. And that's all I have to say about that. Hope it helps. Anyways, if you have a morbid curiosity to join me on this life journey, please feel free to subscribe to this channel and subscribe to my Substack newsletter. If you want to support me in my vlog creation efforts, please become a member of this channel or a paid member of my Substack or just buy me a coffee. If you want a one-on-one coaching session with me, just schedule it. Anyways, thanks so much for watching. Talk soon. Bye.

we've got some noise in here. Now, what we do typically is we do thresholding, right? We can say like if it's above a certain threshold or below a certain threshold, then it's a zero or it's a one. peripheral. And memory-mapped IO is simply reserving a spot in the CPU's main memory where that register that controls that hardware peripheral can be set and changed. And if that's ever changed during the lifetime of my program, that hardware peripheral will update its configuration. This is in contrast to port-mapped IO where the peripheral address space is completely separate. So, it's not in main memory. So, MMIO will waste memory addresses because they have to be reserved to be

mapped to peripheral registers. Port-mapped IO does not have this issue. An example of something that uses port-mapped IO is ATmega GPIO. personal controlled stack memory addresses takes CPU time because what I have to do is when I get my interrupt that says, "Hey, the data is ready," the CPU actually has to waste instructions taking the memory and copying it somewhere else. Because if we don't do that, then the data could get overwritten by the peripheral. So, this is handled by a DMA controller. What a DMA controller does is it's smart enough to be able to take the results from your peripheral and put them straight into a user-specified buffer in main memory. And this speeds things up crazy amounts because the CPU isn't wasting time doing all of these useless copies. And so, here we can see a typical DMA bus. So, we have main memory over here. We have

the DMA controller, the peripheral that we're interested in getting data from, and the CPU. And we all have a shared bus between the CPU, the DMA controller, and the main memory. transfer is done, will we tell the CPU, "Hey, data is ready. You should go and process this." This is really important for performance, and many microcontrollers have DMA controllers built into them, so you don't have to worry about extra peripherals. title: Building an Electric Toyota Pickup Truck in 12 Minutes | Full DIY Build

paragraphs.text: Have you ever looked at an electric vehicle and thought, "Why does it look like a refrigerator? Can it just look normal and cost $30,000 less?" Better yet, have you ever looked at an old car and thought, "Man, if we could shove a bunch of newer technology into this old relic, that'd be really cool." Me too. This is an all-electric 1980s pickup truck. A year ago, I bought this 1982 Toyota pickup. This thing is 44-years old. Back then, these were manufactured with practicality and cost in mind, and you can definitely tell. But, this isn't your average old pickup. Its powertrain is all-electric. So, in this video, I'm going to show you how I took this old pickup truck that I bought with a blown motor and converted it into

an all-electric commuter with mostly recycled parts. Let's get into it. We'll start with a quick overview of the base of the conversion. As I mentioned, it's a 1982 Toyota pickup, and that is literally the model name on the title. It's a regular cab, long bed, two-wheel drive, and best of all, it's a five-speed manual. And it stayed that way. I bought this truck with a clean title and a blown motor, and sadly, the 22R had a rod cap go bye-bye. The truck has some rust in the bed, but the cabin and frame are pretty clean, and I was determined to keep this old truck on the road. So, the first order of business was to remove the old engine and the gas tank. That's pretty easy, just

disconnect some hoses, undo some bolts, edit out about 7 hours of labor, and we have an empty engine bay. Now, how are we going to power this thing? In comes this big DC electric motor that I got off of Craigslist. This is a NetGain Warp 9 DC motor. It's about 140 lbs, has two output shafts, and is rated for 144

volts at 1,000 amps, or 144 kW of peak power. If I was to do this again, I would probably use a Leaf drive unit or some other AC propulsion, but this is what I could find cheaply and locally at this time. But, wait a minute. This thing just has a mangled spinny thing on the front end of it. How's it going to drive the wheels of the truck? I decided that it would be best to leave the manual transmission in place. Yes, this electric truck still has a manual transmission. And honestly, that might be my favorite part of the whole build. I did this for two reasons. For one, because I think it's cool. And two, because I can retain the mechanical advantage of having gears.

And I don't need to do any fancy switching with contactors to get into reverse. I can just shift the transmission into reverse. So, I decided I'd take the clutch out, drill out the rivets, and bolt it to said mangled spinny thing. Now, it just slides onto the transmission, and the motor and the transmission rotate together. It's secured to the transmission using an aluminum adapter plate that I bolted to the motor and the bell housing. For the front mounts, I basically used a bunch of scrap steel angle and welded it in such a way that it bolts up to the stock engine mount. It doesn't look pretty, but it's actually plenty strong. Now that that's done, we're going to dive into some of the more complicated stuff, but in the

interest of keeping this brief and simple, I won't go too deep into the details. I'd be happy to make a more detailed video on each of these parts if people are interested. So, let me know in the comments. First, much like modern gas engines, electric motors need computers to be able to run them properly. For gas engines, these are called ECUs or engine control units. For electric motors, these are simply

called motor controllers. In this instance, my motor controller is just a device that takes input from me, such as the push of the throttle, and pulls power from the battery pack, and sends it to the motor accordingly. It is essentially the middleman between your battery pack and your motor. There are plenty of options for controllers, but I found a good deal on what is widely believed to be the holy grail of DC controllers. Not that that means much in 2026. The Zilla 1K. This was another Craigslist find, so I honestly wasn't even sure if this controller worked, but it seems to be doing great so far. The The needs to be protected from water, so I found this gasketed electrical enclosure on Facebook and decided that's

where all of my controller circuits and chargers would go. It's mounted in the bed so that all the wires can stub through for the necessary connections. I mentioned earlier that the controller receives input from the driver and this occurs in a few different forms. First, I wired it in such a way that

when the key is not on, the car won't move. Pretty smart. I did this by wiring one of the spare ignition fuses to the key switch input on the controller. For my throttle input, I chose to use a throttle pedal from a 2009 Toyota Prius. Naturally, it took a bit of custom

fabrication to get it to fit right, but I was able to make it work. This pedal is safe and redundant and I wired it directly into the controller. You got to love an '80s pickup with drive-by-wire. And of course, aside from the 12-V signal connections, the controller also has high-power connections to the motor and the high-voltage battery pack. The high-power connections to the controller are fused and the connection to the battery also has a main contactor, which is kind of like a big switch. [clears throat] That main contactor is what allows me to turn the vehicle on and off using the original key. And that brings us to our last big piece of the puzzle. Of course, no electric vehicle is complete without a high-voltage battery pack, otherwise

known as the traction pack. Much like the motor and controller setup, there are many, many ways you can build a traction pack. In my case, I chose to use battery modules from an old Tesla Model S. This is a common choice for conversions because they generally have the best energy density around. I only use part of the original Tesla pack, which you can do because the batteries are built from a dozen or so identical modules, depending on the size of the battery in the Tesla. Personally, I used five wired in series to give me a 120-V pack. The pack weighs about 250 pounds and is just over 26 kilowatt hours in capacity. For obvious reasons, I've never

completely drained the pack, but based on similar setups, I estimate around 75 to 85 miles of range. If you're like me and you have everything you need within a couple miles of your house, that should be plenty. This beautiful battery enclosure is from EV West and it's secured to some steel angle that I welded to the frame underneath the bed. Don't worry, it has almost 10 inches of ground clearance and sits about 2 inches above the rear diff. One very important thing about electric vehicle batteries is that they need to be continuously monitored with automated fail-safes in place. This is done using a battery management system or BMS for short. The most common ones for custom

applications are Thunderstruck Motors or Orion BMS. I chose Thunderstruck for their cost effectiveness and good customer support. The BMS is housed within the battery pack and it continuously monitors the temperature and cell voltages of all the batteries in the pack. It shuts everything down if any readings are out of a specified range. The last thing I had to do was figure out a way to charge it and since all of the accessories still run off the 12-volt battery, I need a way to charge both a 12-volt battery and the traction pack. Let's start with the traction pack. My high voltage charger is from Thunderstruck Motors and it is controlled by the battery management system that I mentioned earlier. This device takes 120 volt or 240 volt power in and sends out

about 126 volts to the traction pack. I thought it would be cool to put my charging port where the gas cap was as a little Easter egg. These prongs are not hot, but once you plug the vehicle in, it will automatically start charging. Charging for the 12-volt battery is pretty simple. Since the traction pack is so large, I can pull power from that to top off my 12-volt battery as needed. I did this using a step-down DC-to-DC converter. This one is from, you guessed

it, Thunderstruck Motors. Anytime the truck is on, it takes 120 volts DC from the traction pack and sends about 13 and 1/2 volts to the 12-volt battery to keep it charged. And that covers most of the big ticket items in an electric vehicle retrofit, but there's one more thing I'd like to show you guys, and that is the first time that I took it out for a drive, which I had my girlfriend film against her will. At this point, I had spent months of wiring and troubleshooting trying to get this thing working, and I got to say the payoff when those wheels spun for the first time was pretty great. I was

babying it pretty good with it being the first time on the road and everything, but hopefully you enjoy the following footage which we captured just a few weeks ago. Gabby, would you like to do the honors?
>> Yeah, I'm going to try my best. >> All right. Room for Gabby? >> [laughter] >> You want to jump in? >> Yeah. >> The low-speed control is way better with the Zilla controller.
With the Curtis controller, it would it would jerk around when you if you try to go 1 or 2 mph. Okay. Pretty smooth. We're in first gear. Just barely giving it some throttle. It has a good response.
The Prius throttle works well in this, it seems pretty smooth. Don't mind me, nothing to see here, folks. Just uh normal car. Here we go, to the here. And I'm going to start from second gear. Nice.
It's driving pretty good. What do you think? >> Yeah, it's very smooth. >> I haven't gone much over 25 yet. Uh but I'm not I'm not hearing any funny noises or anything, which is good.

I'm pretty happy with this. >> Yeah. >> Power steering is such an amazing thing. And you don't realize it until you drive without power steering. And it's a total pain in the butt. But that went well, I think. What do you think? >> I think so, too. >> Nice. Wow, what an awful park job. >> You want me to make you a light truck? >> Yeah. Yeah. It's a lot of work. >> I'm wondering what you've been doing in there for the month. >> Yeah.
